fd.shape.title: Numbers with shape and axes
fd.shape.intro: A model works with ordered collections of numbers. The shape gives the number of positions along each axis, not what the numbers mean.
fd.shape.scalar: Scalar: a single number, for example 7. Shape [] has no axes.
fd.shape.vector: Vector: a list, for example [1, 2, 3]. Shape [3] has one axis with 3 components.
fd.shape.matrix: Matrix: a table. Shape [2, 3] means 2 rows and 3 columns: 6 numbers in total.
fd.shape.tensor: Tensor: the general term, including scalars and matrices. [2, 2, 3] can mean 2 tables with 2 rows and 3 columns: 12 numbers.
fd.shape.axes: In this course [B, T, d] means: sequences in a batch, token positions, features per token. d = 3 means 3 coordinates, not 3 words. The axis order must always be stated.
fd.shape.try: Change T and d separately. More token positions add rows; more features make each row wider. The meaning of the numbers is not the geometry of the drawing.
fd.shape.aria: Numbers arranged as a scalar, vector, matrix or two matrices; the result gives the shape and element count.
fd.matmul.title: Shapes that fit together
fd.matmul.intro: Matrix multiplication pairs up two equally long lists, multiplies each pair and sums the products. That is why the inner dimensions must match.
fd.matmul.rule: X [T, d] @ W [d, h] → Y [T, h]
fd.matmul.cause: Each row of X becomes a row of Y. Each column of W produces one component. d is summed over; T and h remain. @ means matrix multiplication, not cell-by-cell multiplication.
fd.matmul.predict: Predict: what shape does [2, 3] @ [3, 2] produce? What is the first number if the first row is [1, 2, 3] and the first column is [1, 0, 1]?
fd.matmul.reveal: Reveal the shape and first calculation
fd.matmul.answer: Four output values. Each output needs all 3 pairs; [2, 3] @ [2, 2] does not work because a pair would be missing.
fd.matmul.orientation: Here token vectors are rows, x @ W. The next lesson also shows the column form W @ x: the same idea, but the matrix orientation and shape must then change.
fd.matmul.aria: Two matrices with fixed outer dimensions; change the inner dimension to test compatibility.
fd.matmul.valid: Compatible: each row of 3 numbers meets a column of 3 numbers. The result has shape [2, 2].
fd.matmul.invalid: Incompatible: 3 components cannot be paired with {{k}}. The product is undefined; it is not a zero result.
fd.sum.title: A weighted sum, step by step
fd.sum.intro: A weighted sum multiplies each value by its weight and adds the contributions. The same calculation can be performed component by component on whole vectors.
fd.sum.cause: The slider transfers weight from v₂ to v₁ without changing the values. Giving the smaller value more weight lowers the sum. With nonnegative weights summing to 1, the answer lies between the values.
fd.sum.attention: This later becomes attention: dynamic weights select how much different value vectors contribute. A mixture is not the same as selecting only the largest weight.
fd.sum.distinction: General learned weights can be negative and need not sum to 1. A weighted sum can then fall outside the interval. The normalized weights here are a special case.
fd.sum.aria: Two values with adjustable weights and a bar showing their weighted sum.
fd.sum.out: {{p}}×2 + {{q}}×6 = {{y}}. The weights sum to 1; the values 2 and 6 do not change.
fd.prob.title: Probability and scores
fd.prob.intro: Probabilities describe mutually exclusive alternatives that together cover all possible outcomes. Each probability is between 0 and 1 and the sum is 1. This is not a guarantee that an answer is true.
fd.prob.relative: In this experiment the masses are nonnegative, like numbers of tickets for A, B and C. Increase A: B and C get less probability even though their masses are unchanged. The denominator is shared.
fd.prob.logits: A logit, in contrast, is an unrestricted score before conversion to probabilities. [-1, 0, 2] are valid logits but not probabilities. Simply dividing these numbers by their sum would give a negative value.
fd.prob.bridge: Softmax in the next lesson first makes the masses positive using the exponential function and then normalizes them. Here we only practise the shared denominator, not softmax.
fd.prob.aria: Probabilities of A, B and C as the mass for A changes; B has mass 3 and C has mass 5.
fd.prob.out: Total mass {{total}}. p(A) = {{a}}, p(B) = {{b}}, p(C) = {{c}}. The sum is 1 before rounding.
fd.state.title: What changes during inference?
fd.state.intro: A weight is a stored setting that the model learns. An activation is a value it calculates for the current input. This tiny model has one weight w and predicts y = x × w. Changing the input and changing the weight are different actions.
fd.state.work:
prediction = input × stored weight
y = x × w
Before training: x = 2, w = 1 → y = 2
fd.state.inference: During inference, the model uses the weight it already has. Move the test-input slider: x and the prediction y change, but w stays fixed. Moving this slider is not training and does not change the learning rate.
fd.state.training: During training, the button compares predictions with three fixed examples: 1 → 2, 2 → 4 and 3 → 6. It adjusts the same weight to reduce their mean loss. Each click performs one update using all three examples—not just the input shown by the slider.
fd.state.cache: This is a constructed one-weight model, not a full LLM. Fixed weights also do not mean a stateless inference server: KV caches, random state and running requests can still change.
fd.state.aria: Current model prediction line and teaching reference, with fixed training examples and the selected test input. Only training updates the weight.
fd.state.out: x = {{x}} → y = {{y}}. Teaching reference: {{target}}; error y − y* = {{error}}. The weight stays w = {{w}}.
fd.attcheck.title: Pause: predict attention
fd.attcheck.intro: Pause after attention. We isolate a single query, two allowed value vectors and already computed attention weights. No new training occurs.
fd.attcheck.predict: Predict both components before revealing the answer. Is the result v₂ because it has the largest weight? If the query gives v₁ more weight, do the learned value-projection weights change?
fd.attcheck.answer: The result is [0.5, 3]: 0.25×[2, 0] + 0.75×[0, 4]. Both components are mixed; the largest weight does not select the entire answer on its own.
fd.attcheck.why: The slider changes a dynamic attention weight, not a model parameter. We hold V fixed to isolate the cause. In a real model, new input can also change Q, K and V.
fd.attcheck.aria: Two value vectors and, after revealing, their component-wise weighted mixture.
fd.attcheck.out: p = [{{p}}, {{q}}] → [{{a}}, {{b}}]. V and the model parameters are unchanged.
fd.mlpcheck.title: Pause: width before the MLP
fd.mlpcheck.intro: Attention has mixed information across allowed positions and written back to the residual stream. The next part will process features within each position. Keep the token axis T separate from the feature axis d.
fd.mlpcheck.predict: Predict: is the intermediate result [5, 3] or [2, 5]? Can we add it directly to X? Is a new set of matrices needed when T changes from 2 to 4?
fd.mlpcheck.answer: First [2, 5], then [2, 3]. Expansion changes the feature width, not the number of positions. Adding to X requires the same shape [2, 3], so contraction must happen first.
fd.mlpcheck.why: With T = 4 the shapes become [4, 5] and [4, 3]. The same matrices are applied to every row. An MLP does not mix token positions; attention handled that part.
fd.mlpcheck.bridge: This is a simplified expand–process–compress model. SwiGLU in the next lesson uses two expansions and a gate. Without a nonlinear function the two matrices could be combined into one.
fd.mlpcheck.aria: Token rows before expansion and, after revealing, wider intermediate results and restored width.
fd.mlpcheck.out: {{t}} rows throughout the calculation. Only the width changes: 3 → 5 → 3. The same parameters are used.
fd.parallel.title: GPU: many workers
fd.parallel.intro: A GPU can perform many similar calculations at once. A matrix product contains many independent output values: these can be distributed among parallel workers. This is not the same as making one worker faster.
fd.parallel.work:
N = 8, t = 1 ms
P = 1 → 8 ms
P = 4 → 2 ms
fd.parallel.dependency: The experiment shows 8 independent jobs. But a later model layer needs the preceding layer’s result, and the next generated token needs the preceding token. Such dependencies cannot simply be distributed away.
fd.parallel.memory: The workers also need numbers from memory. More arithmetic units do not help if they are all waiting for data. Distinguish how many numbers fit, how quickly numbers can be moved and how quickly they can be processed.
fd.parallel.limit: An idealized schedule without overhead, memory waits or uneven jobs. Real GPUs use many more threads and specialized matrix units; this is not a hardware measurement.
fd.parallel.aria: Eight independent jobs distributed among a selectable number of workers; each box takes one millisecond.
fd.parallel.out: {{lanes}} workers, {{waves}} rounds, {{time}} ms. Each job still takes 1 ms.
fd.units.title: Bytes, FLOP and bottlenecks
fd.units.intro: Capacity, bandwidth and compute rate measure different things. A large GPU can fit a model without being able to deliver all its numbers quickly enough.
fd.units.capacity: Capacity: bytes that fit. 8 bits = 1 byte; a bf16 number takes 2 bytes. 3 billion such numbers take 6 GB, before other data.
fd.units.bandwidth: Bandwidth: bytes per second. GB = 10⁹ bytes, GB/s is a rate. GiB = 2³⁰ bytes is a different capacity unit.
fd.units.compute: Compute rate: FLOP/s. A multiplication and an addition count as 2 FLOP here; 1 TFLOP/s = 10¹² FLOP/s. FLOP is work, FLOP/s is a rate.
fd.units.work:
6 GB / 200 GB/s = 0.03 s = 30 ms
120 GFLOP / 4 TFLOP/s = 30 ms
fd.units.bound: For the same hypothetical job, data volume stays at 6 GB and work at 120 GFLOP. The larger of memory time and compute time gives an ideal lower bound. Increase only the faster resource: the bottleneck remains.
fd.units.caveat: The bound assumes data movement and computation can overlap. Real time can be longer due to dependencies, overhead and low utilization. No GPU specification or measurement is used.
fd.units.aria: Two time bars for moving 6 GB and performing 120 GFLOP; the slower resource gives a time bound.
fd.units.out: {{bw}} GB/s → {{mem}} ms. {{fl}} TFLOP/s → {{compute}} ms. Lower bound {{bound}} ms; limit: {{limit}}.
fd.queue.title: Wait, respond, batch
fd.queue.intro: Latency is how long an individual request waits for its result. Throughput is how many results the system produces per second. Eight requests arrive together at time 0; one server serves one batch at a time. We write L for latency, Q for queue time and S for service time.
fd.queue.tradeoff: The invented batch cost S(B) has 20 ms of shared work and 5 ms per request. A larger batch amortizes the shared work and yields more results per second, but the first batch takes longer. Try B = 1 and B = 8.
fd.queue.delay: Extra waiting is added only before the first batch. Here all requests are already present, so that waiting does not help at all. With sparse arrivals, a short collection window can create larger batches, but always costs waiting time.
fd.queue.caveat: Each bar shows a whole request, not a token. Results/s here is not tokens/s. No prefill/decode, variable response lengths or real GPU is simulated. Colored bar = service, thin line = queue time.
fd.queue.aria: Queue and service times of eight requests on a shared time axis; batch size and extra waiting are adjustable.
fd.queue.out: First done {{first}} ms; last done {{last}} ms. Last request: queue {{queue}} + service {{service}} ms. Total 8 / {{seconds}} s = {{rate}} results/s for the entire burst.
fd.quiz.shape.q: What shape does X [2, 3] @ W [3, 4] produce?
fd.quiz.shape.e: The inner 3s must match and are summed over. The outer dimensions 2 and 4 remain: 2 token rows, 4 output components.
fd.quiz.state.q: You change x from 2 to 3 during inference in y = xw with w = 1. What changes?
fd.quiz.state.o1: w changes to 3; y stays at 2.
fd.quiz.state.o2: w and y both stay at 1.
fd.quiz.state.o3: y changes to 3; w stays at 1.
fd.quiz.state.o4: w and y both change to 3.
fd.quiz.state.e: New input produces a new activation y = 3×1 = 3. Inference does not perform gradient updates to w. Cache and other runtime state can still change.
fd.quiz.mix.q: Attention has p = [0.25, 0.75], v₁ = [2, 0], v₂ = [0, 4]. What is the weighted sum?
fd.quiz.mix.e: Sum component-wise: [0.25×2 + 0.75×0, 0.25×0 + 0.75×4] = [0.5, 3]. The largest weight does not select a whole value vector on its own.
fd.quiz.bandwidth.q: A job must read 6 GB. What is the ideal lower bound on its memory time at 200 GB/s?
fd.quiz.bandwidth.e: 6 GB / 200 GB/s = 0.03 s = 30 ms. The byte units cancel, leaving seconds. More memory capacity does not change this rate limit.
fd.quiz.batch.q: Eight requests arrive together. S(B) = 20 + 5B ms. What happens at B = 8 compared with B = 1 without extra waiting?
fd.quiz.batch.o1: The first finishes earlier and the whole burst later.
fd.quiz.batch.o2: The first finishes later and the whole burst earlier.
fd.quiz.batch.o3: Both the first and last finish earlier.
fd.quiz.batch.o4: Both the first and last finish later.
fd.quiz.batch.e: B = 1: first 25 ms, last 200 ms. B = 8: all done at 60 ms. Higher throughput therefore need not give lower latency for the first request.
fd.gloss.scalar.def: A single number. A scalar tensor has shape [] and no axes.
fd.gloss.vector.def: An ordered list of numbers. Shape [d] means d components; each component is a coordinate, not necessarily an interpretable feature.
fd.gloss.matrix.def: A table with two axes. [r, c] means r rows and c columns. In A @ B the number of columns in A must match the number of rows in B.
fd.gloss.tensor.def: An ordered collection of numbers with a shape and zero or more axes. Scalars, vectors and matrices are special cases.
fd.gloss.axis.def: An indexing direction in a tensor, such as token position or feature component. The axis size is the number of positions along it.
fd.gloss.sum.def: Multiply each value by its weight and sum the contributions. For vectors this is done component-wise; in general the weights need not be probabilities.
fd.gloss.probability.def: Probabilities for mutually exclusive outcomes that together cover all possibilities. Values are nonnegative and sum to 1.
fd.gloss.parameter.def: A stored number that can be learned during training, such as a weight or normalization scale. Ordinary inference uses fixed parameters but changing activations.
fd.gloss.bandwidth.def: How many bytes can be moved per second, for example GB/s. This is a rate, not the amount of memory that fits.
fd.gloss.capacity.def: How many bytes fit in a memory. Does not say how quickly they can be read or how quickly computations run.
fd.gloss.queue.def: Time from arrival until service starts. Latency includes both queue time and service time; high throughput does not guarantee short queues.
title.viktad-summa-i-sma-steg: A weighted sum, step by step
fd.state.guide1: Train several steps. Watch the stored weight and the predictions for the fixed examples change together.
fd.state.guide2: Choose inference. The learned weight is now frozen; it is not reset when you switch phases.
fd.state.guide3: Move the input slider. Try 4 or 5, which were not training examples. The model reuses the same weight for the new input.
fd.state.referenceNote: We invented the rule “double the input” to provide teaching answers. The model predicts only x × w; it does not receive the reference 2x as an input. The dashed line is there so you can check its output.
fd.state.sliderHelp: This slider chooses an input number, not the strength of learning. It is locked during training, then moves the test point during inference. It never changes the stored weight or the fixed training examples.
fd.state.trainingHint: Training uses all three fixed examples below. The preview input is locked at x = 2. Press Train one step to update w; this demonstration has {{limit}} visible steps.
fd.state.inferenceHint: The weight is frozen. The slider changes this test input and its displayed reference answer, but performs no weight update. You can return to training without losing the weight.
fd.state.trainingOut: Training step {{steps}} / {{limit}}. w = {{w}}; mean loss on the fixed examples = {{loss}}.
fd.state.lastChange: Last training step: w {{beforeW}} → {{afterW}}; mean loss {{beforeLoss}} → {{afterLoss}}.
fd.state.noTraining: No weight updates yet. The initial weight is w = 1.
fd.state.done: The demonstration’s training sequence is complete. Now try inference with the learned weight.
fd.state.mathTitle: Optional: what one training click calculates
fd.state.mathText: The training button averages the loss gradients from the fixed examples and takes a step with a fixed learning rate. The input slider does not set this rate. Real training uses many parameters and examples; a lower training loss does not guarantee better results on new data.
fd.state.mathFormula:
L(w) = mean( (x·w − target)² / 2 ), x ∈ {1, 2, 3}
g(w) = mean( x·(x·w − target) )
η = 0.1
w_new = w_old − η·g(w_old)
fd.state.probeKnown: This input is one of the fixed training examples.
fd.state.probeNew: This input was not a training example. The simple linear rule is constructed; success here does not prove real-model generalization.
